analysis.one_liner: Keeps paid-off medical bills off credit reports and gives a one-year grace period before unpaid ones appear.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote, after being referred there the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change credit reporting rules for medical debt. Any medical bill that was fully paid or settled would come off credit reports within 45 days. Unpaid medical debt could not be put on a credit report until a full year after the collector sends the patient a notice, and that notice would have to state the exact date reporting can start and remind patients they can still pursue insurance coverage or hospital financial assistance in the meantime. It would not stop collectors from trying to collect; it would only delay and limit what shows up on a credit report.
analysis.who_benefits: People with medical debt — tens of millions of American households, many of them insured — whose credit scores drop when hospital bills land on their reports. A one-year buffer means a bill that gets paid, settled, or covered by insurance during the year never damages the person's credit at all, which protects access to housing, car loans, and employment checks that run credit reports.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical bills in collection

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits credit reports from including any medical debt that was fully paid or settled more than 45 days before the report is issued, erasing the lingering damage from bills that are resolved.

Imposes a one-year waiting period before unpaid medical debt can be reported to a credit bureau, giving patients time to resolve bills with insurers or hospital charity programs before the debt ever appears.

Requires the collector or provider to send the patient a written notice before reporting, stating the specific date the one-year period ends and telling the patient they can seek insurance coverage or financial assistance during that window.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collectors and the three national credit bureaus, which would lose a large category of collection leverage and report data. Medical providers and lenders lose some of it too: providers lose the credit-report threat as a tool to push patients to pay quickly, and lenders lose visibility into a borrower's unpaid medical bills, which some argue forces them to price loans more conservatively for everyone.

drawbacks.text: Legitimate unpaid medical debts would still be reported after the one-year period ends, so the bill shields patients temporarily rather than permanently, and debts still in collection at that point would hit the report just as hard.

Lenders lose access to information about a borrower's unpaid medical obligations, which some in the credit industry argue makes loans riskier to price and could raise costs for other borrowers — even though the bill's own title claims it would make credit markets more efficient.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and well-targeted: medical debt is often the product of an insurance dispute or a billing error rather than financial irresponsibility, and the bill leaves collectors free to collect while simply delaying and then cleaning up what appears on a credit report. The cost to lenders and bureaus is genuine but modest, and the main design limit is that it delays rather than prevents damage from unpaid bills.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2019 in the Senate on May 21, 2019, joined by four Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
That referral was the final action of record: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
All five supporters were Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and debt collectors kept the status quo — medical debt remains a standard item on credit reports, and the credit-report threat remains a collection tool. Patients with medical debt in collections are worse off only in the sense that a fix that had congressional sponsors was never allowed a vote; the committee leadership that controlled the calendar is the actor whose inaction decided the outcome.

against.name: Debt collection and credit reporting industries
against.role: Industries whose business model relies on credit reports as a collection and data asset
against.what_they_did: Had a strong interest in the status quo; the bill's targeted restrictions on medical-debt reporting parallel measures these industries have historically opposed.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote in the Republican-controlled Senate, so no roll-call recorded where the chamber stood.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and medical debt buyers
industries.note: The bill removes the credit report as a first-day collection lever on medical bills: no reporting for a year, advance notice to the patient, and deletion of paid or settled debts. Collectors could still pursue payment, but their strongest pressure tool against patients disappears for twelve months.

The three national credit bureaus would carry fewer derogatory items — paid and settled medical debts must come off within 45 days and new medical debts wait a year. Medical debt is a high-volume, routine feed into their files.

Providers lose the credit-report threat as a way to push patients to pay quickly, but the one-year window steers patients toward insurance claims and hospital financial-assistance programs, which can resolve the bill for both sides.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders and credit card issuers
industries.note: Lenders would no longer see a borrower's unpaid medical bills for the first year, an information loss some in the credit industry argue forces more conservative pricing for all borrowers — though borrowers whose medical debts were wrongly dragging down scores would get cleaner, more accurate credit files.
